title: Sürücü: 'The Drover'; Türk Sazı (1914)
short: A narrative poem of social pity from Yurdakul's Türk Sazı (1914): the poet on horseback, the barefoot boy who leads the animal on foot through the snow.
body: A 'sürücü' is a drover, someone who drives or leads pack animals for hire; here a homeless boy hired to lead the poet's mount. Uçman's encyclopedia article calls Yurdakul (1869–1944) the first great national poet of the Turks: his 'Cenge Giderken' (1897), written during the Greco-Ottoman war in syllabic metre and plain Turkish, is regarded as a starting point for nationalist poetry in plain Turkish and hece, and his aim was to voice the sufferings of ordinary people. 'Sürücü' belongs to that populist (halkçı) side of his work. Uçman also notes the common judgement that his poems are technically weak but were widely popular and historically decisive.

sources.cite: Abdullah Uçman, 'Yurdakul, Mehmet Emin', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, vol. 43 (2013), pp. 613–614

Mehmet Kaplan, Şiir Tahlilleri 1: Tanzimat'tan Cumhuriyet'e Kadar (Istanbul: Dergâh), chapter 'Anadolu'dan Bir Ses yahut Cenge Giderken / Mehmet Emin Yurdakul' (from p. 176 in the current Dergâh printing)

anchor: Gidiyorduk: İri buzlar sarkıtmıştı her saçak
title: Metre: syllabic (hece), 15 syllables
short: The poem is in hece, the native syllable-counting metre: fifteen syllables a line, falling in groups of 4 + 4 + 4 + 3.
body: Count: Gi-di-yor-duk / İ-ri buz-lar / sar-kıt-mış-tı / her sa-çak = 4 + 4 + 4 + 3 = 15. Every verse of the poem keeps this count (in the dialogue one verse is spread over two printed lines), with the pauses (durak) after the fourth, eighth and twelfth syllables. Hece metre, based on the equal number of syllables per line, was the metre of Turkish folk poetry; Yurdakul's choice of it, together with everyday Turkish, was a manifesto against the Persian-Arabic aruz of the divan and of the Servet-i Fünûn. Compare the same scene of snow in Cenab Şahabettin's aruz poem 'Elhân-ı Şitâ' (1897): the two poems show the two roads of Turkish verse around 1900.

sources.cite: Abdullah Uçman, 'Yurdakul, Mehmet Emin', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, vol. 43 (2013), pp. 613–614

anchor: Gidiyorduk: Ben hayvanın üzerinde, o yayan
title: Anaphora and contrast: 'Gidiyorduk'
short: Four lines begin 'Gidiyorduk:' (We were going), and the last two set rider against walker, clothed against barefoot.
body: The repeated verb with a colon is like a refrain in a folk song or a ballad and gives the stanza its slow walking pace. The first two lines set the scene (a narrow path on the snow, great icicles hanging from every eave, 'saçak'), the last two divide the 'we' into two: 'I on the animal, he on foot; I clothed, he poor and barefoot (yalnayak).' The contrast of the comfortable speaker and the suffering child is the structural principle of the whole poem, and it ends by being overcome when the speaker himself begins to shiver.

sources.cite: Abdullah Uçman, 'Yurdakul, Mehmet Emin', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, vol. 43 (2013), pp. 613–614

title: yalnayak, uruba: barefoot, in rags
short: 'Yalnayak' is a colloquial form of yalınayak, barefoot; 'uruba' is the folk form of urba, a garment.
body: Yurdakul draws on spoken, regional Turkish for his effects. 'Yalnayak' (yalın 'bare' + ayak 'foot') is shortened as in speech. 'Uruba', with a helping vowel, is the popular pronunciation of 'urba', clothing, which the Turkish Language Association derives from Italian roba. 'Yırtık pırtık' (ragged), a reduplicated pair, is another colloquial touch. The choice of such words in a printed poem in 1914 was itself a statement, after decades in which poetic Turkish had been mainly Persian and Arabic.

sources.cite: Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük, s.v. 'urba'

title: sefilcik: 'the poor little wretch'
short: Arabic sefil, 'wretched, destitute', with the Turkish diminutive -cik, expressing tenderness and pity.
body: 'Sefil' (Arabic safīl, low, wretched) is one of the few Arabic words in the poem, and Yurdakul turns it Turkish by adding the affectionate diminutive suffix -cik, a device of colloquial and folk speech. The child's body shows through the torn garment, his cracked purple lips, and beneath them, a striking detail, his 'white, beautiful teeth' chattering. The beauty of the teeth among the misery is the one touch that makes the child individual rather than a type.

sources.cite: Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük, s.v. 'sefil'
Abdullah Uçman, 'Yurdakul, Mehmet Emin', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, vol. 43 (2013), pp. 613–614

title: The dialogue and its broken lines
short: The middle stanza is a dialogue between master and boy, marked with dashes and set out in staggered half-lines.
body: The poet asks: 'My son, how much do you get each trip?' 'One metelik.' 'Where is your home? Have you anyone?' 'I have no home, no one.' 'Where do you sleep at night?' 'In the dung heap in the stable; it is warm, it warms me.' The answers break the fifteen-syllable lines into pieces, each continued further along the page, but the syllable count across each full line is kept. Direct, plain dialogue of this kind was new in Turkish verse and shows the influence of narrative realism; the boy's matter-of-fact last words are the most painful lines of the poem.

sources.cite: Abdullah Uçman, 'Yurdakul, Mehmet Emin', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, vol. 43 (2013), pp. 613–614

title: metelik: a quarter-kuruş coin
short: A metelik was a coin worth ten paras, a quarter of a kuruş: proverbially the smallest of sums.
body: The Turkish Language Association defines metelik as an iron coin worth a quarter kuruş, ten paras, and, figuratively, very little money; it derives the word from French métallique. The expression 'metelik vermemek', not to give a farthing, preserves the sense. Yurdakul's companion poem in Türk Sazı, 'On Para Ver' (Give Ten Paras), turns on the same sum, the beggar's plea for a single metelik.

sources.cite: Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük, s.v. 'metelik'

title: The dung heap that warms
short: The homeless boy sleeps in the stable's manure heap because fermenting dung gives off warmth.
body: Rotting manure gives off heat, which is why the boy can sleep in it. The child says it without self-pity: 'it is warm, it warms me'. The realism of the detail, very far from the roses and nightingales of divan poetry, is the point. The poem's later imagined scene, the child trembling 'before which stable' with the wall as his only protection (ll. 17–20), grows out of this answer.

sources.cite: Abdullah Uçman, 'Yurdakul, Mehmet Emin', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, vol. 43 (2013), pp. 613–614

title: From quatrains to couplets
short: The poem moves from cross-rhymed quatrains to rhymed couplets as narration gives way to the poet's emotional reflection.
body: The first three stanzas rhyme abab (saçak / yalnayak; sırtında / altında, yeri / dişleri; alırsın / kalırsın). The last two sections are in rhymed couplets (gününde / önünde; durursun / vurursun; ben / içimden), the commoner pattern of narrative folk verse (mesnevi-like). The opening exclamation 'Ey kimsesiz, sefil çocuk! ben seksen yıl yaşasam / Bu acıklı sözlerini hiç bir vakit unutmam' (even if I lived eighty years I would never forget your words) turns the anecdote into a vow of memory.

sources.cite: Abdullah Uçman, 'Yurdakul, Mehmet Emin', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, vol. 43 (2013), pp. 613–614

title: 'On what stone do you beat, crying "Open!"?'
short: The poet imagines the child at night before some stable wall, beating his hands on stone and begging to be let in.
body: 'Sana karşı duvar olan hangi ahır önünde' means 'in front of what stable that is a wall against you', with 'duvar' carrying both its literal and figurative senses: a wall that shelters and a wall that excludes. The child trembles 'like a hungry, naked beggar' and strikes his hands on stone crying 'Açın!' (Open!). The stone that does not open is the old image of the hard heart, here the society that leaves children outside. The rhetorical questions ('Kim bilir ki...', who knows...) move from report to imagination.

sources.cite: Abdullah Uçman, 'Yurdakul, Mehmet Emin', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, vol. 43 (2013), pp. 613–614

title: Sympathy as physical feeling
short: Beside his warm brazier, the poet feels snow falling on his own body and begins to tremble: 'I am freezing; life is draining from every part of me.'
body: The 'mangal' (Arabic manqal, a brazier of burning charcoal) with its white-ashed coals is the bourgeois comfort that the poem sets against the stable. Yet thinking of the child makes the speaker feel 'something cold' inside, as if snow were falling on him, until he trembles like the boy ('İşte ben de senin gibi titremeye başladım'). The ending turns the opening contrast of rider and walker into identification. Critics may find it sentimental, but it states plainly the populist programme Uçman describes: to make the reader feel the people's pain.

sources.cite: Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük, s.v. 'mangal'
